You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The test `testContainsAnyStringWithSupplementaryChars` fails because `StringUtils.containsAny` does not correctly handle Unicode supplementary characters, represented by surrogate pairs in Java (`\uD840\uDC00` for U+20000). The root cause lies in the implementation of `containsAny`.

The method `containsAny(CharSequence, String)` simply converts the string `searchChars` into a `char[]` and calls `containsAny(CharSequence, char[])`.

In `containsAny(CharSequence, char[])`, the method iterates over the input CharSequence by `char` units (UTF-16 code units), and similarly iterates over the search chars. It compares each `char` from `cs` against each `char` from `searchChars`. If any character matches, it returns true.

This approach fails for supplementary Unicode characters, because such characters are encoded as two `char` values (a surrogate pair) in UTF-16. The code only compares individual `char` values, never considering surrogate pairs as a single code point. As a result, a supplementary character like U+20000 (`\uD840\uDC00`) will not be properly matched, because no single `char` in `searchChars` will ever match the two-part surrogate pair from `cs`.

Hence, the failing test where `containsAny(CharU20000, CharU20001)` expects false behaves incorrectly if a partial match occurs on one surrogate char, or fails to recognize the supplementary characters properly.

The essence of the bug is that the implementation operates on `char` units, not full Unicode code points (int values), and thus mishandles supplementary characters. It needs logic that processes supplementary characters properly, likely by using methods such as `codePointAt()` and adjusting iteration to code points instead of single UTF-16 chars.

Recent bug reports do not relate directly to Unicode or character encoding issues, so they do not provide additional relevant context.

In summary, the bug happens because `containsAny` compares on the basis of single UTF-16 code units rather than proper Unicode code points supporting supplementary characters, resulting in incorrect matching behavior for characters beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane.

Next, I'll suggest the best methods to fix.
org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils.containsAny(java.lang.CharSequence, char[])
org.apache.commons.lang3.StringUtils.containsAny(java.lang.CharSequence, java.lang.String)

Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
